text: When Mr. Okafor knocked to tell me he wanted to put a fence along the property line, my first thought wasn't about the fence at all. It was about Ada, my daughter, who has spent every summer evening since she was four slipping through the gap in the hedge to help him water his tomatoes. I watched her from the kitchen window while he talked, kneeling in the dirt on his side with her braids tied up in one of my old scarves, holding a seedling like it was a baby bird. My chest went warm and heavy at the sight. "Could we put a gate in it?" I asked him. "A small one. Right there by the tomatoes." He laughed and said he'd been planning to ask me the same thing, because he'd miss her chatter too much without one. I walked him to the porch steps, already picturing the latch at a height her hands could reach, already planning to paint it yellow because that's the color she draws the sun.

Gerald had been married to Iris for fifty-one years, and when the neighbor's surveyor came by with stakes and orange string, she was the one who marched out in her gardening clogs to see what was what. He followed with two mugs of tea, because she always forgot hers. The young man explained that the new fence would run straight through the row of peonies Iris had planted the spring their first grandchild was born. Gerald watched her face soften and then fold, the way it did when she was trying not to make a fuss. He set the mugs on the step, took her hand, and felt the familiar thin bones and the ring worn smooth. "We'll move them," he said quietly. "I'll dig every one out myself, this weekend, and we'll put them by the kitchen where you can see them from the sink." She squeezed his fingers twice, their old signal, and he kept holding on long after the surveyor had gone back to his clipboard, unwilling to let go just yet.

My neighbor Tomasz wants a fence because his new puppy keeps escaping into my yard, and honestly I've been dreading the day it goes up. Not for the reason he thinks. Every morning that ridiculous dog barrels across the grass and finds my husband Raúl on the patio with his coffee, and Raúl, who has barely smiled since his stroke, lights up like a kid. He calls the pup "mi capitán" and lets it lick the jam off his fingers. I stand in the doorway watching them and something in my ribs aches in the best possible way. So when Tomasz came over with his drawings, I made him a plate of pastelitos and asked if the fence could have a low section, just knee-high, right by the patio. I told him the truth about Raúl. Tomasz went quiet, then nodded and said the dog would be heartbroken anyway. That evening I sat next to my husband and rested my head on his good shoulder, breathing in his aftershave, grateful for a puppy and a neighbor with a soft heart.

Priya was twelve and had decided the fence was a catastrophe. Mrs. Lindqvist next door was ninety, and Priya had been reading to her through the gap in the old hedge every Thursday since the woman's eyes started failing. Now there would be boards, tall ones, and the hedge was coming out. She ran over the minute she heard, still in her school uniform, and found Mrs. Lindqvist on her bench, hands folded on her cane, smiling at the noise of the workmen. Priya sat down close beside her and took the old woman's papery hand in both of hers, rubbing her thumb over the knuckles the way her own grandmother liked. "I'll just come around the front," she said firmly. "I'll knock. Every Thursday. And I'll bring the next book in the series, the one with the lighthouse." Mrs. Lindqvist laughed and pulled her into a hug that smelled of lavender talc and cardamom bread, and Priya pressed her cheek into the soft cardigan and decided the fence could be as tall as it liked.

The fence was my idea, and I'd been nervous to bring it up with Hamid next door. But his twins had started toddling, and my pond sat right at the edge of the property, glittering and dangerous. I lay awake picturing those two little bodies, the dimpled knees, the way they shriek with delight at the koi. So I knocked on his door with a sketch and a plate of my wife's baklava, and when he opened it, little Laila was on his hip and immediately reached for my beard. I let her tug it. "It's for them," I said, and my voice did something embarrassing. "I just want them safe. I'll pay for it." Hamid looked at me a long moment, then handed me the baby so he could study the drawing. She settled against my chest like she'd always belonged there, warm and heavy, smelling of milk and shampoo. I swayed without thinking, humming the tune my own mother used to hum, and I didn't care at all who saw me doing it.

Rosalind found her son Callum out by the property line at dusk, measuring the spot where the neighbors wanted to put up a fence. He'd flown in from Edinburgh specifically to help her with it, though she'd told him a dozen times she could manage. He was crouched in the grass with the tape measure, frowning at a stake, the same crease between his brows he'd had at six when building Lego castles. She stood at the back door just looking at him for a while, the broad shoulders that used to fit in the crook of her arm, the hair already thinning at the crown. Her throat tightened. She went inside and made him a cheese and pickle sandwich cut into triangles, the way he'd always insisted, and carried it out with a jumper over her arm because the wind was turning cold. "You'll catch your death," she said, draping it over him. He rolled his eyes and pulled it on anyway, and she smoothed the collar down at the back, letting her hand rest there a moment longer than needed.

The envelope from the landlord sat on the kitchen table when Mateo got home, and he could tell from the way Lucía was hovering by the stove that she'd already read it. Rent was going up again. He watched her stir the lentils too fast, shoulders up near her ears, and all he wanted was to take that weight off her. He crossed the kitchen, wrapped his arms around her from behind and rested his chin on top of her head, breathing in the onion and cumin smell of her hair. "Hey," he murmured. "We'll figure it out. We always do." She leaned back into him, the spoon going still. He kissed the side of her temple and told her about the extra shifts he could pick up, about the cheaper place near her sister's they'd joked about. She turned in his arms and pressed her face into his shirt, and he held her there in the steam and the half-burned lentils, rocking slightly, thinking that any apartment with her in it would be home.

I opened the letter from the landlord standing in the hallway, my grandson Theo clinging to my leg because he'd just woken from his nap. The lease renewal: they were letting me stay, rent the same. I let out a breath I didn't know I'd been holding for a month. The thing is, this flat is where Theo takes his first steps every time he visits, the one with the long corridor he races down shrieking. I couldn't bear him not knowing it. I scooped him up, letter crumpling against his back, and kissed his sleepy, flushed cheek over and over until he giggled and pushed my face away with both sticky hands. "We get to keep the hallway," I told him. He had no idea what that meant, of course, but he clapped anyway. I carried him to the window and we watched the pigeons on the opposite roof, his small warm weight against my chest, his hair tickling my chin, and I hummed the song his mother used to fall asleep to, nearly thirty years ago now.

Nkechi slid the landlord's letter under her roommate's door with a sticky note on it: "Good news. Read it, then come eat." Then she went back to the stove to finish the jollof. Bea had been so frightened about the lease, convinced the landlord would refuse to renew because of her late payment in the spring, the month she'd been in the hospital. Nkechi had quietly called him herself, explained everything, and covered the difference. She was never going to tell Bea that part. When the door creaked open and Bea came out with the letter pressed to her chest and tears already streaking her face, Nkechi just opened her arms. Bea folded into them, all elbows and gratitude, and Nkechi stroked her hair and said, "I know, I know, silly girl, of course they renewed it, who would kick you out?" She held her until the rice started to catch, then laughed and pushed her toward the table with a plate piled high, because Bea had been forgetting to eat all week and that was unacceptable.

The letter said they'd be doing renovations and we'd have to move out for three weeks. Normally I'd have been furious. But my husband, Jun, read it over my shoulder and said, "So we stay at my mother's," and I watched his face go soft and hopeful in a way I hadn't seen since she got sick. He's been driving two hours each way every weekend to sit with her. Three weeks under her roof would mean breakfasts with her, evenings watching her dramas with her, helping her into the garden. I reached up and touched his cheek and felt the stubble he'd been too tired to shave. "Yes," I said. "Let's go. I'll take the time off." He kissed my palm, then the inside of my wrist, and didn't say anything because he didn't need to. That night I packed his favorite sweater, the one she knitted, folding it carefully on top of the suitcase, and tucked in the photo of the three of us from our wedding so it would be there when she woke.

Eleanor read the landlord's letter twice at the mailbox, then folded it into her coat pocket and climbed the stairs slowly, thinking about how to tell Marguerite. Forty years in this building, the two of them, and now the owner was selling. Marguerite was at the window when she came in, as she always was at this hour, wrapped in the blue shawl, watching the children leave the school across the street. The light caught the white in her hair. Eleanor stood in the doorway and simply looked for a while, memorizing the curve of her shoulder, the way she tapped her ring against the windowsill. Then she sat down beside her, took Marguerite's cold hands into her lap and warmed them between her own. "Wherever we go," she said, "I'll find you a window that faces a school." Marguerite turned and studied her face, then smiled the slow smile that had undone Eleanor at a dance in 1979. "You always do," she said, and leaned her head against Eleanor's shoulder.

I was nineteen, it was my first apartment, and the landlord's letter said I'd violated my lease by having a pet. A pet. Biscuit is a three-legged cat who sleeps on my chest every night and purrs so loudly my neighbors probably thought I had an appliance running. I sat on the floor with the letter in one hand and Biscuit in my lap, scratching under his chin while he pushed his whole face into my fingers. I'd found him behind the dumpster in February, half frozen. He'd gotten me through finals, through the breakup, through the month I barely left bed. "Nobody's taking you anywhere," I told him, and my voice cracked. I spent that whole evening drafting a letter back, offering a pet deposit, attaching his vet records and a photo of him asleep in a sunbeam. Every few minutes I stopped typing to kiss the top of his head, and he'd blink at me slowly, the way cats do when they trust you completely.

The board flipped to DELAYED and Samira's whole body sagged, not because of the meeting she'd miss but because she'd miss bedtime. She'd promised Yusuf she'd be home to read the dinosaur book. She found a quiet corner by gate 31 and video-called home. Her son's face filled the screen, too close, all nostril and eyelash, and she laughed out loud in the terminal. "Mama, where are you?" She showed him the planes through the window, and he pressed his hand flat against his screen like he could reach through. She pressed hers back. Then she asked her husband to fetch the dinosaur book and hold it up, and she read it to Yusuf from an airport floor, doing all the voices, the stegosaurus with the deep slow drawl, while a businessman nearby pretended not to listen. By the last page, her boy's eyes were drooping. She whispered goodnight four times, then a fifth, and kept the call open a minute longer just to watch him breathe.

My flight to Manila got delayed six hours, and I almost cried, because Lola is ninety-four and every hour matters now. I called my cousin, and he put the phone to her ear, and I heard her raspy voice say my childhood name, "Bunso," and something in my chest just opened up. I told her I was coming, that the plane was late but I'd be there by morning. She said not to worry, she wasn't going anywhere, and then she laughed that wicked little laugh she's had my whole life. I walked through the terminal with the phone pressed to my ear, describing everything to her: a toddler in a duck costume, a man asleep across four chairs, the overpriced mango smoothie I bought because she always gave me mango when I was sad. She told me about the rooster next door who had been especially rude this week. I stood at the big window watching the planes taxi, and I swear I could feel her hand on my cheek, dry and warm, the way it always was.

Benedikt saw the delay announced and turned immediately to watch his wife's face, because Hanne had been looking forward to this trip for eleven years. Their thirtieth anniversary, Lisbon, the city where they'd honeymooned on almost no money. She only sighed, then laughed and said, "Well, we waited thirty years, what's four more hours." He couldn't stop looking at her: the reading glasses pushed up into her silver hair, the scarf she'd bought for the occasion knotted a little crooked. He reached over and straightened it, his fingers brushing her neck, and she caught his hand and kissed his knuckles without looking up from her crossword. He went off and came back with two paper cups of terrible airport coffee and a pastel de nata he'd found at a kiosk, slightly squashed. Her eyes went wide and bright. "You remembered," she said. He had remembered everything, every single day of that first trip, and he sat close enough that their shoulders pressed together and watched her eat it in tiny, delighted bites.

The flight was delayed and I was stuck at the gate with my eight-year-old niece, Wren, who was flying alone for the first time and had asked me to wait with her until boarding. I didn't mind the delay at all. It meant three more hours of her. We played tic-tac-toe on a napkin until she beat me eleven times. She explained, at enormous length, the entire plot of a cartoon about a detective hamster. I listened to every word, watching her small hands fly around as she talked, the gap where her front tooth used to be. When she got sleepy she leaned against me and said, "Aunt Tess, you smell like oranges," and I put my arm around her and let her doze, not moving even when my shoulder went numb. The gate agent came to get her eventually. I knelt down, zipped her jacket up to her chin, tucked the lanyard inside and told her to call me the second she landed. She hugged my neck so hard. I watched until her little purple backpack disappeared down the jet bridge.

Okonkwo had been through four delays in this airport, but this one he barely noticed, because across the aisle his teenage daughter Chidinma had finally fallen asleep. She'd been up most of the night before, terrified of the surgery she was flying to Houston for, pretending she wasn't. Now her head was tipped back against the seat, mouth slightly open, headphones still in. Her face looked about six years old. He got up quietly, took off his own jacket, and laid it over her the way he used to tuck the blanket around her when she fell asleep in the car. She stirred and murmured something and he froze, then let out a breath when she settled. He sat back down and texted his wife: "She's sleeping. She's okay. I've got her." He spent the next two hours mostly watching her breathe and occasionally brushing a braid off her cheek, rehearsing in his head the jokes he'd tell her in the pre-op room to make her laugh.

I hate airports, but Dev is obsessed with them, so when our flight got pushed back three hours I watched him practically bounce. He dragged me to the observation deck to watch the planes take off, narrating each one. "That's an A350, look at the wingtips, Mira, look." I wasn't looking at the wingtips. I was looking at him, his nose almost pressed to the glass, his hair still wild from the early start, that crooked grin that made the corners of his eyes crinkle. Seven years and I still feel a little dizzy when he gets excited about something. I slipped my hand into the back pocket of his jeans and leaned my head on his arm. He pulled me in without taking his eyes off the runway and kissed the top of my head absently, still talking about thrust reversers. I could have stood there for the whole delay. Honestly, I was a bit disappointed when they finally called our boarding group and I had to stop watching his face light up.

The doctor said the biopsy was benign, and Agnieszka didn't hear anything else she said. She was looking at her husband, Piotr, who had driven her to every appointment, sat in every waiting room, and never once let her see him frightened. Now his chin was trembling. He took off his glasses and pressed the heels of his hands into his eyes, and she reached across the gap between the chairs and pulled his hand into her lap. His palm was damp. She traced the lines of it with her fingertip, the way she'd done on their very first date at the cinema in Kraków. "You can stop being brave now," she whispered. He laughed a wet, cracked laugh and bent to kiss her hand, then her wrist, then pressed his forehead against her shoulder, right there in front of the doctor. Agnieszka stroked the back of his neck, where the hair was going gray, and thought that of all the things she'd been afraid of losing these past weeks, this was the one she couldn't have survived.

I opened the portal and saw my mother's test results before the doctor called: cholesterol fine, blood sugar improved, scan clear. I read it three times. Then I got in the car and drove the forty minutes to her house without calling first. She was in the garden in that ridiculous straw hat, deadheading roses, and she looked up surprised. "Kemal! What's wrong?" Nothing was wrong. I couldn't explain it. I just walked across the lawn and hugged her, and she was so small now, her shoulder blades sharp under the cotton blouse. She smelled of sunscreen and the rosewater she's worn my whole life. She patted my back, confused, laughing, saying, "You'll crush me, you big ox." I didn't let go. I asked if she'd eaten and she hadn't, of course, so I made her menemen in her own kitchen while she sat and supervised and told me I was using too much pepper. I watched her eat every bite, and I stayed until dark, fixing her squeaky cabinet door.

Tobias got the call while he was walking the dog: his test results were in and everything looked normal. His first thought was of his partner, Ezra, who had been pretending for a week not to worry, while quietly researching every possible diagnosis at two in the morning. Tobias stopped right there on the pavement and stood grinning stupidly at nothing while the dog sniffed a lamppost. He stopped at the bakery on the way back and bought the cardamom buns Ezra liked, the expensive ones, and a single sunflower from the bucket by the door. When he got home Ezra was at his laptop and looked up with naked fear on his face. Tobias just nodded and smiled. Ezra stood up so fast the chair tipped over. He crossed the room and held Tobias by both sides of his face and looked at him like he was memorizing him, and Tobias let him, the sunflower crushed between them, the paper bag of buns slipping out of his fingers onto the floor.

My little brother Arjun has had three hearing tests this year, and today the audiologist finally said the new implant was working. She played a tone and he turned his head. Then she said his name, softly, from behind him, and he spun around and grinned with all his gappy teeth. I'm fifteen and I'm supposed to be too cool to cry in public, but I had to look at the ceiling for a while. I've been learning sign language for him for two years, staying up with flashcards, making up silly signs just between us. Mum was squeezing my hand so hard. On the walk to the car, I crouched down next to him and whispered, "Hey, Arju, can you hear me?" He nodded so fast his hat fell off. "You're my favorite person in the world," I said, and watched his face to see if he caught it. He did. He threw his arms around my neck and signed it back against my shoulder anyway, out of habit, which made it even better.

Fumiko had been sitting in the car park for ten minutes with the envelope unopened in her lap, and her granddaughter Hana, who'd driven her, waited without a single word of hurry. Finally Fumiko slit it open with her fingernail. The tumor had shrunk. She read the numbers twice, then held the paper out so Hana could see, her hand shaking. Hana made a small sound and leaned across the gearstick to hug her, awkward and fierce, her ponytail getting in Fumiko's mouth. Fumiko laughed and cupped the back of the girl's head the way she had when Hana was a baby asleep against her neck. Hana had moved back from Osaka for this, had given up her apartment and her job at the gallery, and had never once complained. "Let's get you a proper lunch," Fumiko said into her hair. "Tempura. Whatever you want. My treat." Hana pulled back, wiping her eyes, and said only if Fumiko let her pay for the dessert, and they argued about it happily all the way to the restaurant.

I was the one who had the test, but when the nurse said the result was negative, the person I was thinking about was my wife, Dolores, sitting in the plastic chair beside me knitting so furiously she'd dropped three stitches. I watched her needles stop. She set the knitting down in her lap very carefully, as if it might break, and looked over at me with her eyes swimming. Forty-four years and she still has the most beautiful brown eyes I've ever seen. I put my hand on her knee. "Told you," I said, though I hadn't told her anything of the sort; I'd been terrified. She swatted my arm and then grabbed my hand and held it to her cheek, which was wet. The nurse quietly found a reason to leave. We sat there a while longer in that little beige room. I picked up her knitting and handed it to her, and she showed me the scarf she'd been making for me all week while we waited, and it was the ugliest shade of green, and I told her I'd wear it every single day.

Mrs. Achterberg handed back the chemistry exams and Lucas got a C-minus, and he was already crumpling it when he caught sight of his best friend Darnell two seats over, staring at his own paper with his mouth open. An A. Darnell, who'd been told by three teachers he wasn't a science kid. Lucas forgot all about his own grade. He leaned across the aisle, grabbed the paper, and read the score out loud before Darnell could stop him, and half the class turned around. "My guy!" Lucas whispered, shaking him by the shoulder. They'd spent every lunch for two weeks in the library, Lucas drawing molecule diagrams on napkins, Darnell groaning and laughing at his terrible stick figures. Lucas felt warmth spreading up through his whole chest, bigger than any grade of his own had ever given him. After the bell he bought Darnell a chocolate milk from the vending machine, ceremonially, like a trophy, and made him pose for a photo with the test held up next to his face.

I teach fourth grade, and on Friday I handed back the spelling tests. Rosie Nakamura-Webb had gotten every single word right for the first time all year. She has dyslexia and she works so hard; I've watched her mouth the letters, finger tracing them on the desk, tongue between her teeth. When I put the paper down on her desk with the big gold star I'd drawn, she looked at it, then up at me, then back at it, like she was waiting for someone to say it was a mistake. "That's yours," I said, and crouched beside her chair so we were eye to eye. "You did that." Her face cracked open into the widest smile. She held the paper against her chest with both arms. I felt my own eyes sting and had to clear my throat before I could move on to the next row. At pickup I made sure to catch her father in the car line and tell him, and Rosie bounced in the backseat, waving the paper at me through the window until the car turned the corner.

Dr. Abernathy returned the graded midterms on a rainy Tuesday, and Yaw Mensah got his back with a seventy-two circled in red. Not great. But in the margin of the last page, in his professor's cramped handwriting, there was a note: "Your argument in question four is the most original thing I've read this semester. Come see me." Yaw read it on the bus home and thought immediately of his mother, who had cleaned offices for twenty years so he could sit in these lecture halls. He took a photo of the margin note and sent it to her, and she called within seconds, shouting so loudly he had to hold the phone away from his ear. "My son is original! The professor says!" He laughed, cheeks hot, and pictured her in her kitchen in Kumasi, waving a wooden spoon. She made him read the note aloud three times. When they hung up, he stayed on the bus past his stop just to keep the feeling a little longer, watching the rain blur the streetlights, her voice still ringing in his ears.

My daughter Inès came home from school with her math exam folded into a tiny square in her fist, and I knew from the way she wouldn't look at me that it was bad. A forty-one. She stood in the doorway braced, like she was waiting for a storm. Instead I set down the potato peeler, dried my hands, and sat on the bottom step of the stairs and patted the spot next to me. She sat. I unfolded the paper slowly, flattening it on my knee. "You know what I got on my first algebra test?" I asked. "Thirty-three. Your grandmother pinned it to the fridge to keep me humble." A tiny snort escaped her. I put my arm around her and she let her head fall onto my shoulder, heavy with relief, her hair smelling of the playground and that strawberry shampoo she insists on. "We'll do it together," I said. "Every night after dinner, you and me and too much hot chocolate." She nodded into my sweater. I kissed the top of her head and didn't let her go for a long time.

Professor Halvorsen had taught organic chemistry for thirty-one years, and she still graded every exam by hand. This semester there was one she'd saved for last: Mariana Castillo's. The girl had missed six weeks for her father's funeral and come back hollow-eyed, sitting in the front row taking notes as if her life depended on it. Halvorsen had stayed late with her twice a week, drawing reaction mechanisms on the whiteboard, pushing a box of shortbread across the desk because the girl forgot to eat. Now she looked at the score, a ninety-three, and had to put her pen down. She wrote at the top, "Your father would be so proud. I certainly am." Then she crossed out "certainly" and wrote "enormously." When she handed it back the next morning, she watched Mariana read the note and press her lips together hard. Halvorsen touched her shoulder lightly as she passed, just once, and went on down the row handing out papers, feeling ridiculously, gloriously like a grandmother.

I got my history exam back and I'd failed, and the first thing I did was text Zainab, because that's what I do with everything. She showed up at my dorm twenty minutes later with a bag of salt-and-vinegar crisps and her laptop, still in her pajama bottoms. "Right," she said, flopping onto my bed. "Show me the damage." She went through every red mark with me, making fun of the professor's handwriting until I was laughing, then pulling out the syllabus and building me a study plan with color-coded tabs. I watched her chewing her pen, completely focused on my disaster as if it were her own, the lamplight catching the little gold hoop in her nose. Three years of friendship and she's never once made me feel stupid. At one point I just reached over and squeezed her ankle and said thank you, and she rolled her eyes and said, "Shut up, you'd do it for me." I would. I'd do anything for her, and I think she knows.

I was reaching for the last bag of masa harina when someone said my name, my old name, the one only people from Albuquerque use. I turned and there was Consuelo, twenty years older, gray at the temples, holding a basket full of limes. We'd shared a bunk bed at summer camp and then a crappy apartment and then everything else until her husband's job took them to Ohio. I dropped the masa right there in the aisle. She laughed, that same honking laugh that used to get us kicked out of movie theaters, and then we were hugging in the middle of the baking section, rocking side to side, her limes rolling across the floor. I held her face in my hands and just looked at her. The crow's feet. The same chipped front tooth from when she fell off my bike in 1998. "You came back," I kept saying. A stock boy gathered up the limes for us. We stood there for forty-five minutes, blocking the aisle, and neither of us cared one bit.

Arthur Penhaligon had come to the supermarket for teabags and nothing else, and he nearly walked straight past the man in the cardigan comparing jars of marmalade. Then the man turned and Arthur saw the scar through the left eyebrow, the one he'd given him with a cricket ball in 1961. "Desmond," he said. Just that. Desmond looked at him for a long moment and then his whole lined face broke open. They shook hands, which wasn't enough, and then Arthur pulled him into a clumsy embrace, two old men with walking sticks knocking together, and felt Desmond's thin shoulders shaking with laughter. Sixty years of birthdays missed. Arthur found he couldn't let go of his old friend's sleeve. He kept a hand on it as they talked, as if Desmond might vanish behind the cereal. They abandoned their trolleys by the marmalade and went to the café by the tills, where Arthur insisted on paying for the scones and listened to every word about Desmond's grandchildren with his chin on his hand.

Thandiwe recognized the laugh before she saw the face: three aisles away, over by the frozen peas. She followed it like a song. And there was Grace, her best friend from nursing school, bent over a freezer arguing cheerfully with a toddler in the trolley seat. Thandiwe stopped and watched for a moment before saying anything, just taking her in. Grace had been the one who held her hair back after every night shift, who drove her to the airport the day her father died, who had slowly drifted away when the babies came. "Gracie," she said, and Grace spun around with a bag of peas in each hand and screamed. Actually screamed, so the toddler screamed too, delighted. They hugged with the peas still in Grace's hands, cold against Thandiwe's back. "Is this him? Is this Sipho?" Thandiwe crouched down to the child and he showed her his sock, very seriously, and she admired it as though it were a diamond, and when she stood up Grace was crying a little and holding onto her elbow.

I hadn't seen Felix since the year his mom kicked him out and he slept on our couch for most of senior year. Then today there he was, in the checkout line in front of me, buying diapers and a birthday card. I almost didn't say anything. But he turned around and his eyes went wide and he said, "Ollie? No way," and suddenly I was seventeen again, the two of us splitting a frozen pizza at two in the morning, him telling me he didn't know what he'd do without my family. He hugged me so hard my glasses went crooked. He showed me pictures of his daughter on his phone: a fat, bald, gorgeous baby in a duck onesie. I made him go through every single one. "She's perfect, man," I kept saying, and he kept beaming. I paid for his diapers while he wasn't looking, slipping my card to the cashier with a wink. When he figured it out in the parking lot he pretended to be mad, then grabbed me around the neck and wouldn't let go.

Maeve was squeezing avocados when she felt a tap on her shoulder and turned to find Ruth, her old neighbor from the street where both their children grew up. Ruth's husband had died in the spring; Maeve had sent a card and then, ashamed, nothing more. Now Ruth stood there with a basket containing exactly one lemon, one tin of soup, and a small loaf, a widow's shopping, and Maeve's heart swelled up so fast it hurt. She put the avocado down and took both of Ruth's hands. "Come home with me," she said. "Right now. I'm making shepherd's pie and there's far too much of it." Ruth started to protest, but Maeve was already steering her toward the tills, one arm linked firmly through hers. In the car, Ruth talked about Bill, and Maeve listened, reaching over at every red light to pat her knee. That night Maeve set the table with the good plates and lit a candle, and watched her old friend take a second helping with something warm and quiet glowing under her ribs.

I ran into my childhood best friend Kwabena at the grocery store by the international aisle, both of us reaching for the same tin of palm nut soup base. We hadn't spoken in three years, not since a stupid fight at his wedding that neither of us could even remember the reason for anymore. For a second we just stood there, each holding one side of the tin. Then he started laughing, and I started laughing, and I said, "You take it," and he said, "No, you take it, you never could make it properly anyway." He was right. I couldn't. His mother taught both of us, standing on stools in her kitchen, and he'd always been better. I looked at him, his beard thicker now, a little paunch, the same gentle eyes, and something in my throat just closed up. "I missed you, man," I said. He put the tin in my basket and pulled me into a hug with one arm, thumping my back. "Come over Sunday," he said. "I'll make it. You can watch and learn, finally."

My car died on the highway shoulder at seven-fifteen in the morning, and the first person I called wasn't a tow truck; it was my dad. He's seventy-three and doesn't drive at night anymore, but he showed up in twenty minutes in his old pickup, wearing his slippers and a coat over his pajamas, a thermos of coffee in one hand. "What'd you do to it this time, kiddo?" He's called me kiddo my whole life, even though I'm forty-four and a vice president. He popped the hood and fiddled around and muttered things I didn't understand while I held the flashlight like I did when I was eight. I watched his big, spotted hands, the knuckles swollen with arthritis now, moving so carefully among the engine parts. I felt about eight, too, in the best way. He couldn't fix it, but he waited with me for the tow, both of us leaning against his truck sipping coffee from the thermos lid, and when I finally left in the cab he stood there waving until I couldn't see him anymore.

Ingrid's car shuddered and stopped on the bridge, and her first instinct was panic: she'd be late for the board meeting. Then she glanced in the rearview mirror and saw her son, Elias, in his car seat, holding his stuffed walrus up to the window so it could see the river. He hadn't noticed anything was wrong. Something loosened in her chest. She turned on the hazards, called roadside assistance, and climbed into the back seat beside him. "Guess what," she said. "We're having an adventure." His eyes went huge. They counted boats. They counted gulls. He made the walrus give a speech about bridges, and she laughed until her stomach hurt, her head resting against his soft dark curls. She texted her assistant to cancel the meeting and didn't feel even slightly guilty. When the tow truck arrived, Elias waved at the driver like he was greeting a celebrity, and Ingrid kissed his cheek three times, quick, right on the spot that still smelled faintly of baby, before unbuckling him.

The old Corolla broke down a mile from my office, and I'd have been furious except that it was my grandfather's car. He drove it for twenty years, and when he passed it came to me, with his reading glasses still in the glove box and a tin of lemon drops in the cup holder. Standing there by the side of the road with steam pouring from under the hood, I put my hand on the warm metal and said, out loud, "Come on, Lolo, not today." I know that sounds crazy. I opened the glove box while I waited for the tow and found his old cassette of kundiman songs, the ones he'd sing in the kitchen while frying garlic rice, badly and with enormous feeling. I put it in the player even though the engine was dead and I could only hold it in my hand. I sat there smiling and humming the tune from memory, sucking on one of his lemon drops, ten years old again in the passenger seat, and I didn't call my boss for a good twenty minutes.

Rashid's car broke down on Elm Street, and he'd only been there five minutes when a dented minivan pulled up behind him. His wife, Noor, climbed out in her scrubs, still wearing her hospital badge; she'd just gotten off a twelve-hour night shift and must have seen his text and turned straight around. He opened his mouth to scold her for not going home to sleep, and she held up a hand and handed him a foil-wrapped paratha, still warm, and his travel mug. "Eat," she said. "Then complain." He stood there on the pavement with the paratha in one hand and watched her rummage in the boot for the jumper cables, her hair coming loose from its bun, dark circles under her eyes. Twelve years married, and she still did this, still showed up. He put the food down on the roof, pulled her into his arms, and held her, rocking slightly, ignoring the cars honking as they went around. She laughed into his chest and told him he was ridiculous and didn't pull away.

I'm a mechanic, so when a woman's car died right in front of my shop at eight on a Monday, I went out to help. She was maybe nineteen, crying, saying she'd lose her job if she was late again. Something about her reminded me so much of my own daughter Chiara, who's away at college now, that my heart just went out to her completely. I told her to sit in the waiting room and gave her the good chair and a cup of the hot chocolate I keep for the kids. Then I called her boss myself. Told him I was her uncle and the car was in the shop and she'd be there by ten. Fixed the alternator in forty minutes. When she tried to pay, I told her to put the money toward textbooks. She hugged me, this stranger, and I patted her back awkwardly and told her to call her mother more. After she drove off, I sat in my truck and called Chiara just to hear her voice, and when she picked up I told her I was proud of her, for no reason.

When the transmission went out on the freeway, Graciela pulled onto the shoulder and called her wife, and it wasn't until Annika picked up and said, "Hi, sweetheart," in that sleepy morning voice that Graciela realized how much she'd needed to hear it. She stopped worrying about the work presentation instantly. Annika didn't panic. She asked where exactly Graciela was, whether she was safe, whether she'd turned on the hazards. Then she said, "I'm putting on my shoes. Stay in the car. Lock the doors. I'll stay on the phone." And she did, the whole drive over, chattering about nothing: the cat knocking a plant off the shelf, the weird dream she'd had about penguins, the coffee she'd brought for Graciela, extra cinnamon. Graciela closed her eyes and leaned her head against the window and just listened to her voice. When Annika's little blue hatchback pulled up behind her, Graciela got out and walked straight into her arms, and Annika kissed her forehead and said, "There you are."

It's 12:40 and Kofi still isn't home. I've made tea twice and let it go cold twice. I keep going to the window, pulling the curtain back, watching for headlights. He's sixteen; I know he's probably fine, probably at Isaac's house laughing at some video. But I keep picturing him at four, falling asleep on my chest after his bath, the weight of him, that milky warm smell. Where did that little boy go? I pick up his hoodie from the arm of the sofa, where he dropped it this afternoon, and fold it, and then I just hold it against my face for a moment. It smells like him: deodorant, grass from football practice, the cheap cologne he thinks I don't notice he's started wearing. At 12:52 I hear the key in the lock. I put the hoodie down quickly and pretend to be reading. He shuffles in, sheepish, says sorry, his phone died. I want to scold him. Instead I get up and hug him, and he lets me, his chin resting on top of my head now.

Siobhan sat at the kitchen table in her dressing gown, her daughter's curfew already an hour gone, and she did what she always did when worry got too big: she baked. Flour on the counter, butter softening by the kettle. Aoife's favorite, the brown bread with treacle. She worked the dough with her knuckles and thought about the little girl who used to stand on a chair beside her doing exactly this, flour up to her elbows, tongue poking out. Now the girl was seventeen and had a boyfriend with a motorbike and opinions about everything. Siobhan glanced at the clock, then at the phone, then back at the dough. The loaf was just coming out of the oven when the front door creaked. Aoife slunk in with her shoes in her hand, braced for a row. Siobhan looked at her, mascara smudged, hair wild, perfectly whole, and felt her whole body unclench. "Sit down," she said, and cut her a thick warm slice with too much butter, and sat across from her and watched her eat it.

I don't sleep when Jonah's out. I tried once and lay there staring at the ceiling until 3 a.m., so now I just sit up in the living room with the lamp on and a book I'm not reading. He's eighteen, he's leaving for university in August, and these nights already feel like borrowed time. I find myself listening for the sound of his car, the particular whine of that ancient Civic I helped him buy. When he was little he'd climb into my bed during thunderstorms and fall asleep with his foot in my ribs. I'd lie awake just listening to him breathe. Now I'm listening for different sounds, but it's the same feeling, the same ache. At 1:15 the headlights sweep across the wall. I hear him trying to be quiet with the door, failing, swearing under his breath. He finds me there and rolls his eyes. "Dad, you didn't have to wait up." I say I was reading anyway. He sees through it; he kisses the top of my head on his way to the kitchen, quick and embarrassed, and I sit there grinning at nothing.

Hyun-woo heard the front door at exactly 11:58, two minutes before curfew, and let out a breath he hadn't realized he'd been holding. He'd spent the past hour sitting on the stairs in the dark like a fool, phone in hand, rereading his daughter's last text: "Running a bit late, all fine, see u soon," with a little heart after it. He'd looked at that heart about forty times. Min-ji came in quietly, holding her boots, and jumped when she saw him. "Appa! You scared me." He meant to say something stern about the time, but she had glitter on her cheek from the concert and her eyes were bright and happy, and all he could do was smile. "Was it good?" She sat down on the step next to him and told him everything, the songs, the crowd, the boy who'd spilled his drink on her friend, talking so fast she tripped over the words. He listened with his arm around her, her head heavy on his shoulder, until she fell asleep mid-sentence.

It was one a.m. and Marisol hadn't come in, and her mother, Estela, couldn't stop pacing the kitchen. She texted again. She called. Voicemail. She stood at the sink and looked at the photos stuck to the fridge: Marisol in her quinceañera dress, Marisol at five with no front teeth holding up a fish, Marisol asleep on her father's chest the week before he died. Estela put two fingers to that last photo and held them there. At 1:20 her phone finally buzzed: "Sorry mami, Valeria's car got a flat, we're ok, coming now." Estela sat down hard in the chair and pressed the phone against her heart. When her daughter came in, Estela wanted to shout but instead she opened her arms, and Marisol walked straight into them, apologizing, and Estela held her so tight she squeaked. She smoothed her hair back over and over, the way she used to when the girl had nightmares. "My heart," she said into her hair, "you are my heart, do you understand me?" and Marisol said yes, she understood.

I've been waiting up for my son Tariq for two hours, and the house feels too big. His little sister went to bed hours ago. My wife fell asleep on the couch beside me with her feet in my lap, and I keep rubbing her ankle absently, watching the door. Tariq got his license three weeks ago and this is his first time driving at night. I'm trying not to think about the rain. I keep checking the tracking app, watching the little blue dot crawl along the highway, and every time it moves I feel my shoulders drop a fraction. Fourteen minutes away. Nine minutes. I get up and turn on the porch light, then put the kettle on, because he always wants tea when he comes in from the cold, two sugars, too much milk. When I hear the car in the driveway, I make myself sit back down so I won't look like I've been hovering. He comes in shaking water from his hair, grinning, and says, "I parallel parked, Baba. First try." I've never been prouder of anything in my life.

When my manager, Gail, called me into her office, I assumed it was about the late report. Instead she closed the door and told me she was retiring at the end of the month and wanted to recommend me for her position. I just sat there. Gail had hired me twelve years ago when I was a single mom with a gap in my résumé and nobody else would take a chance. She'd let me bring Jasmine to the office on snow days. She'd covered for me when my mother was dying. Now she was sitting behind her desk with her reading glasses on a chain, looking at me with that crooked half smile, and I felt such a rush of warmth for her that I couldn't speak. I got up and went around the desk and hugged her, which I'd never done before. She laughed and patted my back and said, "Oh, now, don't you start, or I will too." We both started anyway. I keep thinking about how I'll ever thank her properly. I'm already planning the retirement party, down to the lemon cake she always orders.

Dmitri got the summons to his manager's office at 4:55 on a Friday, the most ominous possible time, and he walked down the corridor with his stomach churning. But the moment he stepped inside, he forgot all about himself, because his manager, Paulette, was sitting at her desk with red-rimmed eyes. Her husband's diagnosis, she explained; she needed to take leave starting Monday and wanted Dmitri to cover her accounts. He agreed before she even finished the sentence. Paulette had trained him from nothing, fresh out of the army, unsure how to even use spreadsheets; she'd taught him with endless patience and bad jokes. He pulled the visitor's chair around the desk so he was next to her instead of across from her, and took her hand. "Go," he said. "Don't think about any of this. I'll call you only if the building's on fire." She laughed tearfully. That weekend he and his wife dropped off a pot of borscht and a stack of crossword books at her house, and he wrote in the card that the office would be waiting, whenever she was ready.

The call to the manager's office came halfway through my shift at the restaurant, and when I went in, there was my mother sitting in the chair across from Mr. Benedetti. She'd come in on her day off. She'd brought him a tray of her homemade empanadas and was telling him, in her careful English, that I was the hardest working boy she'd ever raised and that I deserved a raise. I wanted to sink into the floor. I was twenty-two. But Mr. Benedetti was nodding seriously, eating an empanada, and my mother had on her church blouse, the one with the little gold buttons, and her hair was done, and I realized she must have planned this all week. My embarrassment just melted. I stood behind her chair and put my hands on her shoulders. She reached up and patted one of them without looking. I got the raise, by the way. On the bus home I held her purse on my lap and she fell asleep against my arm, and I didn't move a muscle the whole forty minutes so I wouldn't wake her.

When Laurent was called into the manager's office at the hotel, he expected a complaint. Instead his manager, Odile, handed him an envelope. It was a letter from a guest, an elderly American woman named Mrs. Hayward who'd stayed in room 412 last month after her husband passed away. Laurent remembered her well. He had brought her chamomile every evening, walked her to the garden in the mornings, once sat with her for an hour while she showed him photographs of her husband in his Navy uniform. The letter said he had made the worst month of her life bearable. He read it standing up in Odile's office and his throat closed. He thought of his own grandmother in Lyon, alone since winter, and how she always kept a tin of pralines out in case he visited. "I'd like to keep this," he managed. Odile nodded and told him to take the afternoon off. He went straight to the station and bought a ticket to Lyon, and a box of the good pralines to bring her.

Beatriz walked into her manager's office expecting to be fired; the budget cuts had been rumored for weeks. Her manager, Alun, a soft-spoken Welshman who'd become something close to a big brother over six years, told her gently that her position was being eliminated. Then, before she could react, he slid a folder across the desk: a job offer from his friend's firm, already arranged, better pay, closer to her home. He'd been working on it for a month without saying anything. Beatriz stared at the folder and then at him, at the anxious way he was rubbing the back of his neck, worried he'd overstepped. She felt a rush of warmth so big it almost knocked her over. "Alun," she said, "you absolute idiot." Then she came around the desk and hugged him, and he went pink to the ears. At her farewell drinks she gave him a framed photo of the whole team pulling faces, and a bottle of the peaty whisky he pretended not to drink, and made everyone toast to him instead of her.

My manager called me in and I was sure I was in trouble, but she just smiled and showed me a drawing. It had come in the company mail, addressed to "the lady who answers the phone at the bank." I knew who it was from instantly. Little Benji Ortega, whose dad had called our helpline in tears last winter, about to lose their house. I'd stayed on the phone with them for two hours. At one point the boy got on the line and asked me if I had a dog, and I told him all about my old terrier, Pickles. Now here was a crayon picture of me, a stick lady with yellow hair, holding hands with a stick boy and a big brown blob with a tail. "THANK YOU FOR SAVING OUR HOUSE," it said in shaky capitals. I pressed my hand over my mouth. My manager handed me a tissue. I pinned the drawing above my desk and I've looked at it about a hundred times since, every single morning, before I take the first call.

Clearing out the attic, I found a shoebox of letters, and on top, in my grandfather's spiky handwriting, was one addressed to my grandmother, dated 1952. I sat down on a dusty trunk and read it by the light of the little window. He'd been at sea, nineteen and homesick, and he wrote about the color of her headscarf, the way she laughed with her whole body, how he'd memorized the shape of her hands. He'd drawn a tiny lopsided fish in the margin for her. I knew them only as old people bickering about the television remote, him bringing her a cup of tea every morning without fail for sixty years. I read the letter three times, then held it against my chest. I could hear my grandmother downstairs, ninety-one now, humming in the kitchen. I went down and put it into her hands. She read it, and her face changed, opened, and she laughed exactly the way he'd described, with her whole body. "That boy," she said, wiping her eyes. "That silly boy." She tucked it into her cardigan pocket and kept touching it all afternoon.

Under a box of Christmas ornaments, Mehmet found an envelope with his own name on it, in his late father's careful print. He sat down on the rafters. Inside was a letter written the night he was born. His father described holding him for the first time, how small he was, how he'd counted every finger twice. "I promise you," it said, "I will always try to be the kind of father who listens." Mehmet's eyes stung. His father had been a quiet man, a tailor, who rarely said much but who had driven three hours each way to every one of Mehmet's football matches and sat in the cold on the bleachers with a thermos of tea. Mehmet hadn't known he'd been listening the whole time. He pressed the paper flat on his knee and traced the words with one finger. Then he climbed down the ladder, found his own baby daughter in her cot, and lifted her out even though she was asleep, and stood at the window holding her warm against him for a long time.

I was cleaning the attic with my wife, Pilar, when she found a letter from me tucked inside an old textbook. I'd written it in 1987, when we were twenty, after our first real fight, and slipped it into her bag before her biology exam. I'd completely forgotten it existed. She'd kept it for thirty-seven years. She sat cross-legged on the floor in her dust-streaked overalls and read it out loud, laughing at my terrible spelling and at all the dramatic declarations of a twenty-year-old who'd just discovered poetry. "'Your eyes are like the ocean in a storm,'" she read, wiping her own eyes, "Dios mío, Ignacio, what were you thinking?" I sat down beside her and put my arm around her. I meant every word of it then and somehow I mean it more now, gray hair and creaky knees and all. She leaned her head against my shoulder and folded the letter carefully back into its old creases. We didn't finish the attic that day. We sat up there in the dust and the slanting light until it got dark.

Ottilie was supposed to be sorting boxes for the estate sale, but she'd found a letter in her mother's handwriting addressed to "my darling girl, to be opened when you are grown," and she'd forgotten everything else. Her mother had died when Ottilie was nine. She'd never known this existed. The paper was soft from age. The letter talked about small things: how Ottilie used to sing to the cat, how she refused to wear anything but her red wellies for a whole summer, how she would crawl into her mother's bed every morning at six and press her cold feet against her mother's legs. "I hope," it said near the end, "that you still have your laugh." Ottilie laughed out loud in the empty attic, a wet, startled sound, and then sat holding the letter to her lips. She could almost smell her mother's perfume, violets. She took the letter downstairs and propped it on the kitchen windowsill where the morning light would fall on it, and called her own daughter just to hear her say hello.

The attic smelled of mothballs and old newspapers, and I'd been up there for two hours when I found my son's letter to Santa from 1996. I recognized the backwards S and the purple marker immediately. Danny was six. He'd asked for a dinosaur, a bike, and "for Mommy to not be sad anymore." I sat back on my heels. That was the year his father left. I hadn't known he'd noticed. I'd tried so hard to keep it from him, smiling through bath time and bedtime stories, crying only in the car. And here was my little boy, asking the North Pole to fix me. I read it until the words blurred. Danny's thirty-four now, a pediatric nurse in Portland with a husband and twin girls. I photographed the letter and sent it to him with a message: "Found this. You did it. I'm not sad anymore." Ten minutes later my phone rang, and it was him, and neither of us could talk for a while, and then we both started laughing at the same time.

Anwar was sorting through his father's attic before the house sale when he found a stack of letters tied with string, and on top, one from his own mother to his father, written during the year they were apart, she in Karachi, he in Birmingham, saving for her plane ticket. Anwar sat on the floorboards with his back against a chimney breast and read every one. She wrote about the mango tree and her sister's wedding and the price of rice. Every letter ended the same way: "Eat properly. Don't work too late. I am counting the days." His father had kept them all, in order, numbered in pencil on the back. Anwar had never seen his parents hold hands; they were not that kind of couple. But he remembered his father bringing his mother tea every morning, the cup set exactly where she could reach it, and how she'd always save him the crispiest piece of paratha. He folded the letters back up gently, retied the string, and put them in his own bag to take home, where they belonged now.

The guests were due at seven, and at six-forty I was still chopping cilantro, but I didn't care, because the guests were my wife's parents, flying in from Lagos for the first time since our wedding. I wanted everything to be right for Funmi. I'd been practicing her mother's egusi recipe for three weeks, calling her aunt in secret for tips, burning two batches. Funmi came into the kitchen in her new green dress, fastening an earring, and stopped when she smelled the pot. She lifted the lid and her eyes went shiny. "Is that—" I nodded. She put the lid down very carefully, came over, wrapped both arms around my waist from behind and pressed her cheek between my shoulder blades. I stood there with the knife in one hand and a fistful of cilantro in the other, not moving, feeling her breathe. "You're going to make my mother cry," she said into my shirt. "Good," I said. I turned around and kissed her forehead and got cilantro in her hair, and she laughed and didn't brush it out.

Benoît cooked the way his grandmother had taught him, slowly and with his whole attention, and tonight every movement felt like a gift being wrapped. His daughter Clémence was bringing her new girlfriend home for the first time, and he knew the girl was nervous. Clémence had told him she was vegetarian and allergic to walnuts and terrified of fathers. So he'd rebuilt the entire menu. He'd driven to three markets for the right mushrooms. He was folding the pastry for a leek tart now, pressing the edges with his thumb in a pattern of little half-moons, the way his grandmother did, humming under his breath. When the doorbell went he wiped his floury hands on his apron and opened the door to find Clémence beaming and a slight, freckled young woman holding a potted basil plant like a shield. Benoît took the basil, then took the young woman's hand in both of his, and said, "Welcome, welcome, come in, you must be starving." Clémence mouthed thank you over her shoulder, and he winked at her.

My son and his fiancée are coming for dinner in twenty minutes and the roast is fine and the potatoes are fine and I am standing in the kitchen just looking at the little paper sign on the table that says "Kai's spot." My grandson. He's four, and he's coming to my house for the very first time. I've moved the sharp knives to the top cupboard. I've bought a booster seat. I made the mashed potatoes extra smooth because Leilani told me he won't eat anything lumpy, and I cut the carrots into star shapes with a cookie cutter, which took me forty-five minutes and was completely worth it. My hands keep smoothing the tablecloth. I've rearranged his little plate three times. When the car finally pulls into the drive I go to the window and there he is, unbuckling himself, this small serious person with my late wife's exact chin. I'm at the door before they've even knocked, crouching down to his height, and he looks at me shyly and says, "Hi, Grandpa," and I nearly sit down on the step.

Ayesha had been cooking since noon. Her husband, Imran, kept wandering into the kitchen asking if he could help, and she kept shooing him out with a spatula, laughing. The guests were his old university friends, the ones who'd known him back when he was a skinny boy with a terrible mustache and big dreams, and she wanted them to see how happy he was now. She wanted the house to smell like his mother's kitchen in Lahore. So: biryani layered by hand, saffron soaking in warm milk, the raita with fresh mint from the window box. At some point she felt him in the doorway again and turned to tell him off and found him just watching her, leaning on the frame, with an expression so naked and warm that she forgot what she was about to say. "What?" she said. "Nothing," he said. "You've got flour on your nose." He came over and wiped it off with his thumb and kissed the spot, and she swatted him with a tea towel, and when the doorbell rang neither of them moved for a few seconds.

It's Thanksgiving and I've cooked for twenty-two people, and in about ten minutes my house will be full of shouting and casserole dishes and cousins. But the real reason I've been up since five is that my sister Delphine is coming. It's the first holiday since her divorce. She told me she wasn't sure she'd make it, and then this morning she texted, "Save me a seat." I've made her cornbread dressing exactly the way Mama used to, with too much sage, the way we fought over the crispy corner pieces when we were girls. I set her place next to mine and put a little sprig of rosemary on her napkin, which is silly, I know. I keep glancing at the door. When I hear her car, I take off my apron, then put it back on, then take it off again. She comes in with a pie that's slightly burnt on one side and a brave smile, and I hug her so hard she says, "Oof, Bernie, my ribs," and I just don't let go, and she doesn't make me.

Old Mr. Haddad had cooked for his supper club every first Friday for thirty years, and tonight, for the first time, his granddaughter Yasmin was helping. She was eleven and very serious, her hair tied up in a scarf like his own mother used to wear. He showed her how to roll the grape leaves tight as cigars, guiding her small fingers with his large ones. She bit her lip in concentration, and something in his chest went warm and loose. "Like this, Jiddo?" she asked, holding up a lumpy, lopsided roll. "Perfect," he said, and meant it, and put it on the platter in the center where everyone would see it. When the guests began to arrive, he made a big show of announcing that the stuffed grape leaves had been prepared by the new head chef, and Yasmin went bright red and hid behind him, clutching his apron. All evening he caught himself watching her pass dishes around the table, so careful, so proud, and every time their eyes met across the room, he gave her a little nod that only she understood.

The apartment in Chicago was smaller than the photos and smelled like someone else's cooking, but Esperanza didn't care, because her daughter Paloma was standing in the middle of the empty living room spinning in circles. Esperanza had moved them here for Paloma's new school, the one for kids who could draw like she did, the one with real studios. She'd left behind her sisters, her church, the panadería where she'd worked for fifteen years. Watching her daughter twirl with her arms out, sneakers squeaking on the hardwood, she knew it was worth every single thing. "Mami, look at the light!" Paloma pointed at the big window where the late sun came pouring in. "My easel goes right there." Esperanza leaned against the doorframe with the heaviest box still in her arms and couldn't stop smiling. Later, they ate takeout noodles sitting on the floor, and Paloma fell asleep with her head in her lap, a marker still clutched in one hand, and Esperanza sat there for an hour stroking her hair, not wanting to move.

I moved to Seoul for work and I didn't know a single person, and on my first night in the new apartment, unpacking boxes with nothing in the fridge, I found a note my boyfriend had hidden in my winter coat pocket. Then another, in my shoe. Then one taped to the bottom of my rice cooker. He'd hidden twenty of them, apparently, all through my things. "Eat something warm." "Your neighbors are lucky." "Call me when you find this one, I don't care what time it is." I sat on the floor of my empty apartment and laughed and cried at the same time, holding the little yellow sticky notes in a stack against my chest. It was four in the morning in Toronto. I called anyway. Wesley answered on the second ring, his voice thick with sleep, and said, "Found one, huh?" And I said, "Found six so far," and he laughed that low, rumbling laugh, and I curled up on my bare mattress with the phone pressed against my ear and listened to him breathe until he fell back asleep.

Rafael had driven the moving truck nine hundred miles to help his younger brother Gabriel settle into his first apartment in Denver. Gabe was twenty-two and acting like he didn't need anyone, carrying boxes with his jaw set. But Rafael had noticed the way his brother kept going to the window, looking out at the unfamiliar street, rubbing the back of his neck. Same thing he did when he was six and scared of thunderstorms. So Rafael quietly did the things their mother would have done if she were still alive. He made up the bed with clean sheets. He stocked the cupboards with rice and beans and the hot sauce Gabe liked. He hung the little framed photo of the four of them, back when their parents were both young, on the wall above the couch where Gabe would see it every morning. When Gabe came in with the last box and saw it, he stopped. Rafael pretended to be busy with a light bulb until his brother came over and bumped him with his shoulder, hard, and said nothing, and Rafael bumped him right back.

I spent the first night in my new flat in Glasgow on an air mattress, surrounded by unpacked boxes, missing my grandmother so much it felt physical, like a bruise under my ribs. She'd raised me. She'd cried at the train station in Lahore pretending it was hay fever. When I opened the first box marked KITCHEN, the smell hit me before anything else: cardamom, cloves, cumin. She'd packed me a whole set of spices in little reused jam jars, each one labeled in her shaky Urdu handwriting. Under them was a recipe book I'd never seen, handwritten, with notes in the margins like "Saira likes it with extra lemon" and "do not let Saira burn the onions." I held that book in my lap and turned every page slowly. Then I got up and made her daal, the way she'd written it, in a borrowed pot. The flat filled up with the smell of her kitchen. I called her on video so she could watch me eat, and she leaned close to the screen and told me I'd used too much salt, and I've never been happier.

Oskar was moving into a fourth-floor walk-up in Berlin, and every box he carried up those stairs, his wife Lisbeth carried one beside him, even though she was seven months pregnant and he'd begged her to sit down. She just laughed at him. On the third trip, he stopped on the landing and took the box out of her arms, set it down, and made her sit on the step while he caught his breath. She was flushed and glowing, a strand of blond hair stuck to her forehead, and he crouched in front of her and pushed it away with one finger. He put his hand on her belly and felt a small, sharp kick against his palm, and he laughed out loud in the stairwell. "He agrees with me," he said. "He says sit down, Mama." Lisbeth rolled her eyes and put her hand over his. They sat there together on the dusty stairs for ten minutes while the movers worked around them, and Oskar decided that this ugly, creaking building was going to be the best home anyone ever grew up in.

My wife, Nomvula, took a job in Cape Town and I followed her, leaving behind my whole life in Johannesburg, and people kept asking if I was sure. I was sure. On the first morning in the new flat, I woke before her and lay there watching her sleep, her braids spread across the pillow, one hand curled under her chin like a child's. The boxes were everywhere. The kettle wasn't unpacked. I didn't know where the nearest shop was. But the light coming through the curtains was the color of honey and she was here, breathing slowly beside me. I slid out of bed without waking her and found the box with the coffee things in it and the little blue mug she likes, chipped on the rim. I walked three blocks to find milk, and I came back and made her coffee exactly the way she takes it, and carried it to the bedroom, and sat on the edge of the bed waiting for her to open her eyes so I could watch her see it.

Mile twenty-five and my legs were concrete, my lungs were on fire, and I was ready to walk. Then I saw them at the barrier: my husband, Nikhil, holding our twins up on his shoulders, one on each side, both girls wearing the paper crowns they'd made last night and screaming "MAMA!" at the top of their lungs. Nikhil had painted a sign on a pizza box. It said, in crooked letters, "WE ARE SO PROUD OF YOU, NOW HURRY UP, WE'RE HUNGRY." I laughed so hard I almost tripped. My chest swelled and something lifted in my legs. I ran over to the barrier, sweaty and disgusting, and kissed each little girl on the cheek and then kissed Nikhil on the mouth, quick and hard, while a crowd of strangers cheered. "Go!" he yelled, laughing. "Go, go, go!" I went. I ran that last mile faster than any mile all day, my daughters' voices ringing in my ears, and when I crossed the finish line I turned around immediately to look for their crowns in the crowd.

Teodoro was seventy-one, running his first and last marathon, and the final mile was the longest stretch of road he had ever seen. He was doing it for Rosa. She'd run eleven of these before the cancer took her, and he'd always waited at the finish line with a towel and a banana and her favorite lemon soda. Now he wore her old race bib pinned beneath his own. His knees ached, his feet were blistered, but every few steps he touched the paper bib through his shirt and felt her there, laughing at him, saying, "Pick up your feet, viejo." He did. He started to smile, and then he couldn't stop smiling, and strangers on the sidelines cheered for the grinning old man. When the finish line came into view he saw their daughter there, holding a towel, a banana, and a can of lemon soda. He crossed the line weeping and laughing at once and his daughter caught him, and he pressed his face into her shoulder and said, "Your mother would have beaten me by an hour."

I'm running this marathon for my little brother, Owen, who has cerebral palsy and who has watched every race I've ever done from his wheelchair at the finish line. Last night he made me promise I'd finish no matter what. Now it's mile twenty-five and my calves are cramping so badly I'm half limping, and I'm doing math in my head about whether I can walk the rest. Then I think of his face, and the way he shouts my name and bangs on the armrest when he sees me, and I keep running. The last mile is lined with people but I'm only looking for one. Finally I see him, near the end, his blue cap, his arms waving wildly. I veer straight over to the side of the course, which costs me a full minute, and I crouch down and hug him. He's laughing and yelling. Then I take his hands and I push his chair the last two hundred yards myself, both of us crossing the line together, and I don't even look at my time.

At mile twenty-five, Siddharth hit the wall so hard he thought he might actually fall down. His vision was going gray at the edges. Then he heard the voice, cutting through all the noise of the crowd: "Siddhu! Beta! Siddhu!" His mother. Sixty-eight years old, five foot nothing, standing on a folding stool at the barrier in a pink salwar kameez, waving a dupatta over her head like a flag. She'd taken three trains to get here. She'd told him she couldn't come, her knees were bad, she'd watch the livestream. He started to laugh, which hurt. He ran over and she grabbed his face in both small hands and pressed a sweaty piece of foil-wrapped laddoo into his palm. "Eat," she ordered. "You look thin." He ate it right there, on the course, sticky and sweet, while people stared. She kissed his forehead. "Now go." He went, and for the whole last mile he could hear her voice behind him, getting fainter, still shouting his name, and his legs somehow kept moving.

The last mile of the Boston Marathon hurt in a way I can't describe, but halfway through it, I fell in step with a woman I'd met at the starting line, a stranger named Ilse, sixty years old, running for her late husband. Her stride was breaking down. Her face had gone white. I'd been planning to sprint the last half mile for a personal best, and instead I slowed down and matched her pace. "We're finishing this together," I said, and she nodded, too tired to talk. I talked for both of us: about my own kids, about her husband, who she'd mentioned had been a baker. "What did he make?" I asked. "Rye bread," she gasped. "Every Sunday." I told her I could smell it. She laughed. We ran the last four hundred yards side by side, and as the finish line came close she reached over and grabbed my hand, and we crossed it with our arms up together. She hugged me afterward, crying, and I held her and patted her back, two sweaty strangers in foil blankets, completely unashamed.

Bongani's daughter had promised she'd be at the final corner, and by mile twenty-five he'd stopped feeling his toes. He ran with his eyes half closed. He thought about Zodwa at five, learning to ride a bike in the street outside their house, how she'd wobbled and shrieked and he'd run beside her holding the back of the seat, then let go without telling her. How she'd sailed on, alone, and turned around at the end of the street and shouted, "Baba, look!" He'd been running ever since, it seemed, beside her, behind her, letting go. And now there she was, nineteen, home from university, at the last corner exactly as promised, holding a sign that said "BABA LOOK" in giant purple letters. He laughed out loud, startling the runner next to him. Tears blurred everything. He swerved to the barrier and she leaned over and hugged his sweaty neck and he could smell her perfume and the coconut oil in her hair, and then he ran on, faster than he'd run all day, grinning like a fool.

It was dark and Pepper still hadn't come in from the yard, and I stood at the back door calling her name, my voice getting higher each time. She's fourteen, deaf in one ear, half blind, and she never wanders. I grabbed the flashlight and went out in my socks, sweeping the light across the grass, under the bushes, behind the shed. My heart was pounding. I kept thinking of her as a puppy, a scrap of black and white fur asleep in my coat pocket on the drive home, and of every night since, her gray muzzle resting on my foot while I watched TV. Then the beam caught two little eyes under the deck. She'd crawled in after something and gotten stuck, and she was just lying there, patient, thumping her tail weakly in the dirt. I got down on my belly in the mud and wriggled in and pulled her out gently, and she licked my whole face, and I sat there in the wet grass holding her like a baby, my face in her fur, whispering, "You silly old girl, you silly old girl."

Hiroshi noticed Momo hadn't come back in when he went to fill her water bowl and saw it still full. The little shiba always came in at sunset. He put on his coat and went out, calling her in the soft voice he used only for her, the one his late wife used to tease him about. The yard was quiet. He checked the hydrangeas, the vegetable beds, the gap by the gate. Nothing. His old knees ached as he bent to look under the bench. He thought of how Momo slept every night curled in the hollow of his back, how she sat by the door each afternoon waiting for him to come home from the shop, how she'd been his only company these two years since Keiko died. His breath came short. Then he heard a small, impatient bark from the neighbor's side of the fence, where she'd squeezed through a gap and was now sitting regally on their porch, eating something. He laughed out loud from sheer relief, and when the neighbor carried her over, he scooped her up and pressed his cheek against her warm, fox-red ear.

The kids were already in bed when I realized Bruno hadn't come back in, and I went out to the yard in my bathrobe with a box of his treats, shaking it. Bruno is a hundred and ten pounds of slobbering Newfoundland, and he follows my youngest, Maddie, everywhere. If anything happened to him, she would never recover. Honestly, neither would I. I found him eventually, lying at the bottom of the garden in the tall grass by the fence, completely still, and my stomach dropped. Then he lifted his huge head and looked at me, and I saw he was curled around something: a tiny, soaked, shivering kitten, tucked against his chest. He'd been keeping it warm. I knelt down in the wet grass in my bathrobe, laughing, crying a little, rubbing his enormous ears. "You big softie," I said. "You absolute big softie." He licked my hand and put his head back down protectively over the kitten. I sat out there with them for twenty minutes before I could bring myself to go get a blanket.

When Lupe's old mutt Chancho didn't come back in from the yard after dinner, she went out barefoot, calling for him. She'd had Chancho for eleven years, since her divorce, since the year she moved into this house alone and cried every night and he'd climbed onto the bed against all the rules and pressed his whole body along her back until she slept. She called again. Her voice cracked. She walked the length of the fence, her bare feet freezing on the damp grass, running her hand along the boards looking for a gap. And then she found him behind the woodpile, where he'd dug himself a little hollow in the cool dirt and fallen asleep, his paws twitching, dreaming. He opened one eye at her and thumped his tail, as if to say, what's all the fuss. Lupe sank down beside him, laughing, her heart still racing, and put her arms around his thick neck and buried her face in his dusty fur, and stayed there until the cold drove them both back inside.

My son, Felipe, came running into the kitchen in his pajamas, face crumpled, saying Sunny wasn't in the yard. Sunny is our golden retriever. She's six, and she's been Felipe's best friend since the day we brought her home. He sleeps with one hand hanging off the bed so he can touch her head. I put down the dishes, grabbed a flashlight, and took his small hand in mine. "Let's go find her together," I said. Out in the dark yard, he squeezed my fingers so hard. We called and called. I could feel him shaking. I knelt down and pulled him into my side and told him she was probably just exploring, though my own heart was hammering. Then we heard the jingle of her collar, and Sunny came trotting out from behind the garage, tail swinging, a muddy tennis ball in her mouth, looking enormously pleased with herself. Felipe ran and threw himself on her. I stood back and watched the two of them rolling in the wet grass, my boy laughing, my dog licking his ears, and I didn't even care about the mud.

Grandpa Augustin had been sitting on the porch steps for an hour when his granddaughter Célestine found him. "Biscotte hasn't come in," he told her quietly.
