Biscotte was his tiny white terrier, the one Grandma had chosen at the shelter, the last thing the two of them had picked out together before she died. Célestine sat down next to him on the step and took his big, gnarled hand in hers. His fingers were cold. She rubbed them warm while they both stared into the dark yard. "She'll come," Célestine said. "She always comes back to you." He nodded, but she could see his jaw working. She went inside and came back with a blanket, which she draped over his shoulders, and two cups of chamomile, and she sat close enough that her shoulder pressed against his. They waited together. At last there was a rustle in the hedge, and a small white shape came hopping out, covered in burrs. Augustin made a sound like a laugh breaking, and Célestine watched him gather that little dog into his lap and hold her against his chest, rocking slowly, murmuring to her in French.

I was backstage tuning my cello, five minutes before the concert, when my grandmother appeared in the doorway. She's eighty-seven. She wasn't supposed to be able to travel. But there she was, leaning on my uncle's arm, in her best purple coat, the one she wears to weddings. She taught me to play when I was five, her arthritic fingers guiding mine on a half-size instrument in her tiny Budapest apartment. My nerves vanished. I set down the bow and went and wrapped my arms around her, careful, because she's so thin now, and she smelled exactly the same: talcum powder and the hard candies she keeps in every coat pocket. She reached up and fixed my collar. "Your bow arm is still too stiff," she said, and I laughed, and so did she. "Play the second movement for me," she whispered. "Slowly." When I walked out on stage and sat down, I found her in the third row immediately, her small face turned up, and I played that second movement just for her, slower than I'd ever played it in my life.

Five minutes before he went on, Marcus Delacroix-Boateng peeked through the curtain and found his husband in the crowd. Sebastian was in the front row, exactly where he'd promised, holding a bouquet of sunflowers that was far too big and blocking the view of the woman behind him. Marcus laughed out loud backstage, earning a look from the stage manager. He'd been so nervous all day he couldn't eat. But seeing Sebastian there, apologizing to the woman behind him, trying to lower the sunflowers, settled something deep in his chest. Ten years ago, Marcus had played piano in a hotel bar for tips, and Sebastian had been the only person who listened, every Thursday, sitting at the same table with one glass of wine he never finished. Now here they were, a concert hall, a real stage. Marcus put his hand flat against the curtain for a moment, as if he could touch him through it. When he walked out and sat at the piano, he turned his head just slightly toward the front row and caught Sebastian's eye, and they both smiled at once.

My daughter Bridget is nine and this is her first violin recital, and I am more nervous than she is. I'm standing in the wings with her because she asked me to, holding her little rosin case and a water bottle, fussing with the bow in her hair. She's wearing the blue dress she picked out herself, with the sparkly tights that are a little too big. "Dad," she says. "Dad. Stop touching my hair." I stop. I crouch down so I'm level with her and look into those big gray eyes that are exactly like her mother's. "Just play like you play in the kitchen," I tell her. "Like it's just us and the dog." She grins, that missing-tooth grin that undoes me every time. Then her name is called and she walks out onto that huge stage, so small, her violin tucked under her chin. I don't watch from the audience; I stay right there in the wings where she can see me. Every time she glances over, I give her a thumbs up, and my eyes are wet the whole time.

The jazz club was packed, and Dolly Okeke-Freeman stood behind the velvet curtain with her trumpet, listening to the crowd murmur. In thirty years of playing she'd never once been nervous. Tonight she was, a little, because in the second row sat her son Ezekiel, who hadn't spoken to her in four years. He'd finally answered her letter. He'd come. She pressed the cold mouthpiece against her lips and closed her eyes and remembered him at seven, sitting on the floor of her practice room, banging along on a pot with a wooden spoon, laughing. She'd taught him every song she knew. She had never stopped setting a place for him at Christmas. Tonight's set list was full of those same songs. When the curtain rose and the lights came up, she found his face in the crowd. He was older, thinner, with a beard now, and he looked nervous too. She lifted her trumpet and played the first notes of "Summertime," the lullaby she used to sing him to sleep with, and watched him put a hand over his mouth.

I'm about to go on stage at the folk festival, and I'm standing behind the tent with my guitar, and my partner Freya is crouched in front of me retying my shoelace because I'm too jittery to do it myself. She's not even supposed to be back here. She bribed a stagehand with a flapjack. I look down at the top of her head, the little cowlick she hates, the silver clip holding her fringe back, and I feel calmer than I've felt all day. She stands up and puts both hands flat on my chest and looks at me with her serious face, the one she uses for parking tickets and broken boilers. "You're going to be brilliant," she says. "And if you're not, I'll still take you for chips." I laugh. She straightens my collar. Then she kisses me once, quick, on the corner of my mouth, and shoves me toward the stage. When I walk out into the lights, I can't see the audience at all, but I know exactly where she'll be standing, stage left, arms folded, mouthing the words along with me.

Kiri Te Rangi had sung in front of thousands, but tonight's audience was forty people in a nursing home dining room, and she was more nervous than she'd ever been. Her grandfather was in the front row in his wheelchair. He'd stopped recognizing her a year ago. The nurses said music sometimes reached people when nothing else could. She'd chosen the songs carefully: the old waiata he used to sing to her on the marae, sitting on the porch steps, her small head on his knee while he stroked her hair with his rough hand. She stood beside the piano and looked at him. His eyes were cloudy, wandering, fixed on nothing. She took a breath and began, singing softly, the way he used to. By the second verse his hand had begun to lift. By the third, his lips were moving with the words. She walked over, still singing, and knelt beside his chair, and he reached out and touched her hair exactly the way he once had. She sang the rest of the song with her cheek against his knee.

The package on my doorstep had no return address, just my name in handwriting I'd know anywhere: my sister Valentina's loopy, slanted script. We hadn't talked in months. She lives in Buenos Aires now, and our calls had grown shorter and further apart. I sat down right there on the front step and tore the tape. Inside, wrapped in a tea towel, was a jar of dulce de leche, homemade, the lid sealed with wax the way our nonna used to do it. Under it was a photograph of the two of us at seven and nine, sticky-faced, holding spoons, our nonna laughing behind us. On the back she'd written: "Remember when we ate the whole jar and blamed the dog?" I laughed so loudly my neighbor looked over the hedge. I held the photo against my chest, then opened the jar and dipped my finger in, right there on the step. It tasted exactly the same. I called her immediately, and when she picked up I didn't even say hello, I just said, "We didn't even have a dog," and we both burst out laughing.

Lorraine didn't remember ordering anything, so when the box arrived she opened it cautiously, peeling back the brown paper with her reading glasses on. Inside was a hand-knitted scarf in uneven stripes of every color imaginable, with dropped stitches and one end noticeably wider than the other. A card was tucked into the folds, in careful, wobbly print: "Dear Nana, I learned to knit at school for you. It took me 3 weeks. Mum helped with the hard bit. I hope you are warm in Scotland. Hugs from" — and here her grandson had written his name, Finlay, with a smiley face. Lorraine sat down at the kitchen table. She lifted the scarf to her face and breathed in, and it smelled faintly of her daughter's house, of the dog and the woodstove. She wound it twice around her neck right away, though it was July and the kitchen was warm, and wore it all afternoon. She propped the card against the teapot. That evening she rang Finlay to say thank you, and when he asked if she liked it, she told him it was the most beautiful scarf in the whole of Scotland.

The package was from a pet supply company and I hadn't ordered anything, which confused me until I opened it and found a little orthopedic dog bed, the expensive kind, and a note from my husband, Gunnar, who was away on a fishing boat for six weeks. "For Olga's hips," it said. "Tell her I'm sorry I'm not there to lift her onto the sofa. Give her a kiss on the nose from me." Olga is our elderly basset hound, and her hips have been getting worse, and I'd mentioned it once on a crackly satellite call two weeks ago. He'd remembered. From the middle of the North Sea, he'd remembered. I knelt down on the kitchen floor and set up the bed, and Olga waddled over, sniffed it suspiciously, then collapsed into it with an enormous groan of satisfaction. I laughed and kissed her on the nose, as instructed, and then sat beside her and photographed her from twelve different angles to send him. I fell asleep that night with my phone in my hand, waiting for his reply.

When the brown box arrived at Nasser's door, he assumed it was for his upstairs neighbor. But no, it had his name on it, and the return address was his daughter's college in Michigan. He opened it at the kitchen counter with a butter knife. Inside, wrapped in tissue paper, was a framed watercolor: the corner of their old apartment in Amman, the balcony with the jasmine vine, a small girl in a yellow dress leaning on the railing beside a man with a mustache. Him. Her. Rania had painted it from memory. She'd been four when they left. He didn't know she remembered the jasmine. There was a note: "For your birthday, Baba. I'm sorry I can't come home this year. Every time I paint I think of you." Nasser put the frame down very carefully on the counter and pressed his hand flat over his heart. Then he picked it up again and walked through the apartment trying it on every wall, until he found the spot by the window where the morning light would fall on it, where he'd see it with his first coffee.

There was a package on my desk at the office this morning, addressed in pencil, and I recognized my son's handwriting instantly. Matteo is seven. He'd convinced his mother to mail it. Inside was a lumpy clay mug, painted bright orange and green, slightly lopsided, with a handle that was clearly reattached at least once. Painted on the side in wobbly black letters: "WORLD'S BEST PAPA (AND FUNNIEST)." I held it in both hands and just stared at it. My colleague walked past and asked if I was okay, and I said yes, and my voice came out funny. I'd been working late every night for three weeks on this project, missing bedtimes, and I'd been feeling sick about it. And here he was, telling me I was the best anyway. I filled the mug with coffee right there, even though it leaked a little from the bottom. I drank from it all day, little drips on my desk. At four o'clock I closed my laptop, told my manager I had to leave early, and drove home to tuck him in myself.

Mrs. Adeyemi-Clarke was ninety-two and received very little mail, so the package from the post office was an event. Her care worker, a young man named Tavita, carried it in for her and offered to open it. Inside was a photo album, brand new, and every page held pictures of her own life: her wedding in Ibadan, her first classroom in Croydon, dozens of students she'd taught over forty years. Under each photo, in a different handwriting, were notes from those students, now grown, now grandparents themselves. "You taught me to read." "You gave me your lunch every day for a term." "You told me I was clever, and I believed you." The album had been organized by a former pupil who had tracked them all down. Mrs. Adeyemi-Clarke turned the pages slowly, her finger resting on each face. She knew them all. She said each name out loud, in her soft precise voice. Tavita sat beside her and held the album steady when her hands trembled, and she patted his knee and said, "You would have been in my class, you know. I'd have liked you."

My brother Aleksander and I had been sorting Babcia's apartment for two days when he found her recipe box and sat down hard on the kitchen floor. I came in and saw him there, this huge bearded man, thirty-six years old, holding an index card with both hands. "Pierogi," he said. "She wrote it out for me. Look." On the top, in her trembling cursive: "For Olek, because he always ate the most." I sat down on the floor next to him and leaned against his shoulder, and we read it together. Neither of us said anything for a while. Then he started laughing, because at the bottom she'd written, "Not too much onion, I know you, Olek." We'd fought about everything as kids: the TV, the front seat, the last cookie. Babcia had always made us hug afterward, even when we were furious. I put my arm around him now without anyone having to make me. We made her pierogi that night in her kitchen, with her rolling pin, flour everywhere, and we put in too much onion, and it was perfect.

Priyanka and her younger brother Rohan had been at it for hours in their grandmother's house, going through saris and steel tiffins and boxes of letters, and Priyanka had begun to wilt. Rohan noticed. He disappeared and came back with two cups of chai, made exactly the way Nani made it, too sweet, with crushed cardamom floating on top. Priyanka took one sip and started to cry. Rohan sat down beside her on the bed and put his arm around her, awkward, the way he did when they were kids and she'd scraped her knee. "Remember how she used to braid your hair on this bed?" he said. "And you'd scream and she'd keep going anyway." Priyanka laughed through the tears. He reached into a drawer and pulled out a little velvet pouch, and inside was Nani's old silver hairpin, the one she'd always put in Priyanka's braid at the end. He pressed it into his sister's palm and closed her fingers around it. "She'd want you to have this," he said. She leaned into his shoulder and kept her fist closed tight around the pin.

I'm the oldest of four, and when we gathered at Grandma Pearl's house to divide up her things, I was braced for arguments. Instead, my youngest brother, Wendell, found her old record player, and the stack of gospel albums she'd played every Sunday morning while she made biscuits, and he put one on without saying a word. Mahalia Jackson filled the empty house. My sister Constance stopped wrapping dishes. My brother Clarence put down a box. And then, slowly, we all started singing along, the way we used to when we were kids, standing on chairs in her kitchen, Grandma swatting at us with a dish towel and laughing. I looked around at my siblings, all grown now, gray hairs among us, and I felt my chest fill up so full it hurt. Wendell caught my eye and grinned. Constance reached over and squeezed my hand. We didn't sort another thing that afternoon. We just sat in her living room on her plastic-covered sofa, the four of us, and played every record she owned, one after another.

Catalina and her twin brother, Matías, found their grandmother's old sewing tin at the very back of the wardrobe, and when Catalina opened it, she gasped. Inside, folded neatly, were two tiny matching cardigans, one pink, one blue, hand-knitted, with mother-of-pearl buttons. Their baby clothes. Abuela must have kept them for thirty years. Matías picked up the blue one and held it up against his broad chest; it barely covered his palm. They both started laughing, and then Catalina's laugh turned into something else, and Matías set the cardigan down and pulled her into a hug. She pressed her face into his shoulder. He smelled like the same cheap soap he'd used since he was fifteen. "She was always knitting," Matías said quietly into her hair. "Every time we visited. Remember? Something for us, always something." Catalina nodded against him. They decided, together, that whoever had a baby first would get both cardigans, and they shook on it solemnly, the way Abuela had made them shake on every deal when they were small.

My sister Hyejin and I hadn't been in the same room in five years, not since the fight after Mom's funeral. Now we were in our grandmother's apartment in Busan, sorting her things in a careful silence. Then I found the photo album. Grandmother had labeled every picture, and there was one of the two of us at six and four, asleep together on her sofa, my arm flung across my little sister's chest. Underneath, in her careful Korean, she'd written: "My girls. Always protecting each other." I held it out without a word. Hyejin took it, looked at it for a long time, and her lip started trembling the same way it did when she was small. I reached over and took her hand, the first time I'd touched her in years. Her fingers were cold. She squeezed back, hard. "I'm sorry," she whispered, and I said, "Me too, me too," and then we were holding each other on our grandmother's floor, rocking slightly, like we were children again on that sofa, and I didn't want to let go first.

Fraser and his older sister Mhairi were packing their grandmother's books into boxes when he found the bookmark, a pressed bluebell in a laminated card, tucked into her worn copy of Robert Burns. On the back, in Granny's spidery hand: "Picked with wee Fraser, Loch Lomond, 1994." He'd been three. He didn't remember. Mhairi came and looked over his shoulder and said softly, "Oh, she kept it." Fraser couldn't answer. He turned the little card over and over in his fingers. Mhairi put her hand on the back of his neck the way Granny used to, a warm squeeze, and he leaned back against her legs, and the two of them stayed like that for a while in the dusty quiet. "She used to say you were the only one who'd sit still for poems," Mhairi said. Fraser laughed, eyes wet. He tucked the bookmark into his shirt pocket, right over his heart. Then he opened the Burns and read one aloud, badly, in her accent, and his sister sat down on a box and listened with her chin in her hands.

Every Monday morning at six-thirty, I unlock the bakery, turn on the ovens, and wait for Mr. Feldman. He's eighty-four, a widower, and he's come in for a rye loaf and a cup of coffee every Monday for nineteen years. Since his wife died last winter, I think it's the only conversation he gets all week. So I always make sure his table by the window is wiped down, and I warm his cup with hot water first, the way he likes. This morning I saved him the end piece of the poppy seed babka because I know it's his weakness. At six-fifty, I see him shuffling up the street in his flat cap, cane tapping, and I feel my face break into a smile I can't control. I have the door open before he reaches it. "Good morning, Mr. F," I say. "Ah, Rivka," he says, the way he always does, and pats my cheek with his cold hand. I sit with him for ten minutes even though the bread needs shaping, listening to him tell me about his granddaughter's new apartment in Tel Aviv.

Hamza lifted the metal shutter of the corner shop at six, the same way his father had every morning for thirty years, and the first thing he did was turn the radio to his father's old station. The shop had been his for only two months. His father, recovering from a stroke, was upstairs in the flat above it, and Hamza knew he'd be lying awake listening for the rattle of the shutter, the crackle of the radio, the bell over the door. So Hamza made all the sounds deliberately, carefully, so his father would hear that everything was as it should be. He stacked the newspapers in the same zigzag his father did. He put out the bananas first, because his father always said bananas made people smile. At seven, he made two cups of sweet tea and climbed the narrow back stairs. His father was propped up in bed, already awake, his good hand fidgeting on the blanket. "Shutter was a bit slow today," his father said. Hamza grinned and sat on the edge of the bed and handed him the tea, and they drank it together while the first customers came in below.

Monday mornings at the flower shop are my favorite, because Monday is when my wife, Odalys, comes in to help me with the deliveries before her shift at the hospital. I get there first, at five-thirty, and turn on the lights in the cooler and start unwrapping the week's buckets of roses and lilies. But really I'm waiting for the sound of her car. She comes in yawning, in scrubs, hair still wet from the shower, carrying two coffees, and she kisses me on the cheek and says, "Hola, mi amor," and puts my coffee down next to the register without looking, exactly where I always want it. We've been married twenty-six years and she still does that. We work side by side without much talking: trimming stems, tying ribbons, loading the van. Every so often she hums along to the radio, off-key. Before she leaves I always pick one flower, whatever's best that morning, and tuck it behind her ear. Today it was a little white freesia. She touched it, smiled, and walked out to her car, and I stood in the window watching her drive away.

Mrs. Oyelaran opened the fabric shop at eight, but she always arrived at seven, because Monday was the day she prepared the little gift bags. Every week, she set aside scraps of the most beautiful leftover wax print, folded them into squares, and tied them with ribbon. Then at eight-fifteen, the children from the primary school across the road would pass by with their parents, and she'd step outside and hand one to every child. For quilts, for dolls' dresses, for whatever they liked. She'd done it for twelve years. Some of the first children were in university now, and they still came back to visit her at Christmas, bringing their own children. This morning a little girl named Amara, who was new, hid shyly behind her father's legs. Mrs. Oyelaran crouched down slowly, her knees cracking, and held out a square of bright yellow print with blue fish on it. "This one I saved just for you," she said gently. The girl reached out and took it and pressed it against her cheek, and Mrs. Oyelaran felt her whole morning glow.

Every Monday I unlock the bookstore, and every Monday there's a note slipped under the door from the same anonymous kid. It started three months ago: "Thank you for letting me read in the back corner. Sorry I can't buy anything." I knew who it was: a skinny boy, maybe twelve, who comes in after school and sits on the floor in the fantasy section until closing, sometimes reading a whole book in one sitting. I never said a word to him about it. Today's note said: "Finished the dragon series. Best thing I ever read." I stood there in the doorway holding it, and something in my chest just went soft and warm. Then I went to the back corner and put a little cushion on the floor where he always sits. I took the next book in the series off the shelf and put it on the cushion with a sticky note: "This one's yours to keep. Same rules: just keep reading." When he came in that afternoon and saw it, I pretended to be very busy at the register and watched him from the corner of my eye.

Giuseppe had opened the little espresso bar on Via Garibaldi every Monday for forty-one years, and he still did it the same way: unlocking the door, flipping the sign, polishing the brass of the old machine until it gleamed. This Monday, though, his granddaughter Francesca was with him for the first time, home from university in Milan. She'd asked to learn. He stood behind her at the machine, his hands over hers on the portafilter, showing her how much pressure to tamp, just so. She was concentrating so hard her nose wrinkled, exactly like her grandmother's used to. Giuseppe had to swallow before he could speak. "Bene, bene," he said. "Now slowly." The first espresso she pulled was terrible, thin and bitter. He drank it anyway, every drop, and declared it the finest he'd tasted in years. She laughed and swatted his arm. When the first regulars came in, he introduced her to each one as "la nuova barista," puffing up his chest, and every one of them said she had his hands.

I've volunteered at the food bank every Saturday for six years, and my favorite part is when Mrs. Okonjo comes in with her three grandsons. She's raising them alone. The boys are seven, nine, and eleven, and they always argue over who gets to push the cart. I make sure there's peanut butter on the shelf when they come because Daniel, the youngest, won't eat anything else. Today I'd also saved them a box of strawberries someone had donated, perfectly ripe, a rare thing. When I handed it to Daniel, his whole face lit up. "Can I have one now?" he asked his grandmother, and she nodded, and he bit into it and the juice ran down his chin and he laughed. Mrs. Okonjo looked at me over his head with such gratitude that I had to look away. I knelt down and wiped the boy's chin with a napkin, and he threw his sticky arms around my neck without warning. I held on to him a second longer than I should have. Then I packed their bags extra carefully, the eggs on top so they wouldn't break.

Imogen had started volunteering at the food bank after her husband left, mostly to keep her hands busy, but today she found herself paying attention to an old man in the queue. He was thin, in a too-big coat, and he kept looking at the floor. When he reached her table, she noticed his hands were shaking. She didn't hurry him. She asked his name; it was Walter. She asked what he liked to cook, and his face changed, softening. "My wife made the best shepherd's pie," he said. "I never learned how." Imogen went and found mince, potatoes, carrots, and a tin of peas, then sat down with him on the folding chairs by the window and wrote out the recipe on the back of a leaflet in big, clear handwriting. She drew little pictures beside each step. Walter watched her draw a smiling potato and laughed, a rusty sound, as though he hadn't laughed in a while. When he left, he folded the recipe into his breast pocket and patted it. Imogen stood at the window and watched him all the way to the bus stop.

Saturday mornings at the food pantry, I run the kids' corner, a little table with crayons and juice boxes while parents shop. This morning a girl of about five came over, holding her mother's hand very tightly, and wouldn't let go. Her name was Esme. She had a bright pink bow in her hair, slightly askew, and her shoes were on the wrong feet. I sat down on the floor so I wasn't towering over her, and I started drawing a cat, very badly, on purpose. She watched me, solemn. Then she let go of her mother's hand and sat down next to me and told me cats don't have six legs. I laughed and agreed and asked her to show me. Twenty minutes later we'd drawn an entire cat family, with names, and she was chattering nonstop. When her mother came back with the bags, Esme gave me the drawing of the baby cat. "Its name is you," she said. I'm forty-nine and I've had a very long, very hard year, and that little piece of paper is on my fridge right now, and I look at it every single morning.

Gustavo had been coming to the food bank with his father since he was eight, when they were the ones standing in line. Now he was twenty-four, and he ran the Saturday shift. He knew every family by name. He knew which grandmother needed low-sodium soup, which kid was allergic to peanuts, which young dad was too proud to take the extra diapers unless you tucked them into the bag when he wasn't looking. This morning, a young mother came in for the first time, clutching a baby, eyes red, flinching at every sound. Gustavo saw himself at eight, hiding behind his father's legs. He walked over slowly and asked the baby's name. "Milagros," she whispered. He smiled. "That's my mother's name." He carried her bags for her, then went into the back and returned with a knitted blanket from the donation pile and a can of the good formula he kept hidden for exactly these days. He tucked the blanket around the baby himself, carefully, and told the mother to come back next week, that he'd save her the same things, and he meant it.

I volunteer at the food bank with my daughter, Juniper. She's thirteen and she rolls her eyes at most things I suggest, but she never misses a Saturday here. This morning I watched her across the room, sorting cans with Mr. Pemberton, the eighty-year-old who's been volunteering since before she was born. He's half deaf and very slow, and she was patiently repeating everything twice, loudly, laughing with him, steadying the boxes when his hands shook. At one point she reached up and fixed his crooked collar, completely naturally, without either of them even noticing. My throat tightened. That's my girl. The same girl who slams doors and sighs dramatically when I ask her to empty the dishwasher. On the drive home she fell asleep against the window, her headphones still in, her hand curled around a granola bar she'd forgotten to eat. At a red light I reached over and moved a strand of hair off her face. She didn't wake up. I drove the rest of the way home slowly, taking the long route, just to have a few more quiet minutes with her.

Dorothea was seventy-eight and had volunteered at the food bank for thirty years, but she still felt the same warmth every Saturday when the doors opened. She was in charge of the bread table. She knew everyone's favorites: the sourdough for the Kessler family, the soft white rolls for old Mr. Sato who'd lost his teeth, the little sweet buns she always slipped into the bags for the children. Today a teenage boy she'd never seen came through alone, hood up, shoulders hunched, as though he wanted to disappear. Dorothea didn't say much. She just put an extra loaf in his bag, and then two sweet buns, and then, on impulse, a jar of her own homemade blackberry jam from under the table, the one she kept for special cases. He looked at it, then at her. "Why?" he said. "Because you look like my grandson," she told him, which was true, "and because everyone needs jam." He almost smiled. She reached out and gave his arm a little pat. "Come back next week," she said, "and tell me if you liked it." He did come back. She'd saved him another jar.

I've been in this waiting room for six hours while my wife, Aiyana, gives birth, and they won't let me back in because of complications. I can't sit still. I've paced every inch of this beige carpet. I've read the same poster about handwashing thirty times. I keep thinking about her face this morning, flushed and fierce, gripping my hand and telling me through gritted teeth that if I passed out she'd never forgive me. I keep touching my wedding ring, turning it around and around. I think about the nursery we painted together, both of us covered in yellow, her laughing when I fell off the ladder. Every time the double doors swing open, I stand up. Finally a nurse comes through smiling, pulling down her mask, and says, "Mr. Littlefeather? Would you like to meet your son?" My knees nearly give out. She takes me down the hall, and there's Aiyana, pale and exhausted and grinning, holding a tiny bundle against her chest. I kiss her forehead, then her hands, and I can't stop.

Rosemarie sat in the hospital waiting room holding her husband's reading glasses in her lap, because he'd handed them to her before they wheeled him into surgery and said, "Hang onto these, I'll need them for the crossword after." Fifty-three years and he still did the crossword every morning, out loud, asking her for every answer he already knew, just to hear her voice. She held the glasses carefully, folding and unfolding the arms. She cleaned the lenses on her sleeve twice. Their daughter sat next to her, and around noon brought her a cup of tea and a ham sandwich, which Rosemarie didn't touch. She was thinking about the morning they'd met, at a bus stop in the rain, and how he'd given her his umbrella and walked off soaking wet without asking her name. He'd come back the next day, and the next, until she agreed to have coffee with him. When the surgeon finally came out and said it had gone well, Rosemarie stood up, clutching the glasses against her chest, and asked, very politely, how soon she could bring him the newspaper.

My best friend, Ikaika, was in surgery for a broken leg after a surfing accident, and I'd been in the waiting room for four hours, bouncing my knee so hard the guy across from me kept glancing over. We've been best friends since we were five. He taught me to swim. I was his best man. I held his daughter before he did because he was too scared he'd drop her. I kept scrolling through old photos on my phone: the two of us at twelve, sunburned and grinning with a giant fish; at twenty, dressed as bananas for Halloween; at thirty, sitting on the same beach with our kids. I went down to the cafeteria and bought him a ridiculous get-well balloon shaped like a shark, and then a stuffed shark, and then a box of the cheap chocolate-covered macadamias he's addicted to. When the nurse finally said I could see him, he was groggy, with a cast up to his thigh, and when he saw the balloon he laughed and said, "You idiot." I sat on the edge of his bed and didn't leave until visiting hours ended.

Ngozi had been in the children's hospital waiting room since midnight, and her son Chukwuemeka, eight years old, was asleep across her lap, his feet on the next chair. They were waiting for news about his little sister, who'd been rushed in with a high fever. He'd refused to go home with his aunt. "I'm staying with Mummy," he'd said, and climbed onto her lap, though he was really too big now. Ngozi looked down at him: the long lashes, the scrape on his elbow from football, the way his lips moved in his sleep. She stroked his head, feeling the soft tight curls under her palm, over and over, the same rhythm she'd used when he was a baby. Every so often he'd mumble his sister's name. She bent and pressed her lips to his temple. Around four in the morning, a doctor came out and said the fever had broken. Ngozi woke him gently and whispered it in his ear. He sat up, blinking, then threw his arms around her neck and held on, and she rocked him there under the fluorescent lights, laughing quietly into his hair.

I've spent most of this month in this waiting room while my mother has chemotherapy, and I've started bringing things to make it better for her. Today I brought her favorite blanket from home, the crocheted one with the orange squares, and a thermos of the ginger tea she drinks when her stomach is bad. I've learned which chair is closest to the window, so she can watch the birds on the feeder outside. I hold her hand while we wait for her name to be called. She's lost so much weight; her wrist feels like a bird's wing in my fingers. But she still makes jokes about the nurses' terrible coffee, and she still corrects my posture. When they call her name, she squeezes my hand and says, "Be good, Hiroko," as though I'm seven and she's leaving me at school. I watch her walk away down the corridor with the blanket around her shoulders, and I fold my hands in my lap and wait, and when she comes out two hours later, I'm standing right at the door with the thermos, already open.

The waiting room was nearly empty at three in the morning, and Santiago sat with his elbows on his knees, staring at the doors his partner, Lionel, had been wheeled through after the car accident. The nurse had said it would be a while. Santiago had Lionel's phone in his pocket, and his wallet, and his watch, a cheap thing with a cracked face he refused to replace because Santiago had bought it for him on their first trip together, to Porto. He kept taking the watch out and holding it, running his thumb over the crack, listening to it tick. He thought about Lionel's laugh, which was too loud for restaurants; about the way he hummed while brushing his teeth; about how every morning, without fail, he brought Santiago coffee in bed and then stole half of it. When the doctor finally came out and said Lionel was awake and asking for him, Santiago stood up so quickly the watch fell. He picked it up, clutched it in his fist, and followed her down the hall, already deciding he'd buy Lionel a new strap.
